```{r setup, include = FALSE, purl = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
# the code of the benchmark is in the script code/operations_benchmark.R, from
# which the chunks below are read (purl = FALSE because pkgdown purls this
# file from the package root when looking for images, where this relative
# path does not exist)
knitr::read_chunk("code/operations_benchmark.R")
# the results of the benchmark, saved by the script
benchmark <- readRDS("benchmark-results.rds")
```

`tidytracks` works on `move2` objects, and many of its functions do what
other packages for tracking data also do. This article compares how long
`tidytracks` takes for three common operations with other packages that
offer them:

- the distance between consecutive locations of each track (step lengths),
  with `move2` (Kranstauber et al. 2024), `amt` (Signer et al. 2019) and
  `trip` (Sumner 2011);
- the speed filter of McConnell et al. (1992), with `trip`, from which
  `tidytracks` ported it;
- splitting the tracks of a central place forager into trips away from its
  nest, with `track2KBA` (Beal et al. 2021).

It also checks that, given the same settings, they give the same results,
and shows how the time of each operation grows with the length and the
number of the tracks.

The [results](#results) come first. The second part,
[How the benchmark was run](#how-the-benchmark-was-run), describes the
simulated tracks and the benchmark, with their code, and how to run it again.

# Results

```{r results_packages, include = FALSE}
# to summarise and plot the results
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r data_set_roles, include = FALSE}
series_tracks <- benchmark$series$tracks
series_total <- benchmark$series$total
# the two data sets on which the packages are compared: a few long tracks
# (the data set in both series), and ten times as many tracks of medium
# length (with the same number of locations in all)
long <- c(tracks = series_tracks, locations = series_total / series_tracks)
medium <- c(
  tracks = 10 * series_tracks,
  locations = series_total / (10 * series_tracks)
)
```

```{r check_numbers, include = FALSE}
checks <- benchmark$checks
# the value of a check, summed over all the data sets
check_total <- function(operation, package, check) {
  sum(checks$value[
    checks$operation == operation & checks$package == package &
      checks$check == check
  ])
}
# a count, with a comma for thousands, for the text and tables
count <- function(operation, package, check) {
  format(check_total(operation, package, check), big.mark = ",")
}
# the largest relative difference between step distances (in %), over all
# the data sets
distance_diff <- function(package) {
  100 * max(checks$value[
    checks$operation == "distance" & checks$package == package
  ])
}
# the text below assumes that the distances of trip and tidytracks are the
# same (up to rounding errors), that all the tracks in which tidytracks and
# trip flag different locations have an outlier as their second-to-last
# location, and that tidytracks and track2KBA put the same locations in
# trips, except at the ends of trips and tracks
stopifnot(
  distance_diff("trip") < 1e-7,
  check_total(
    "speed_filter", "trip", "tracks with locations flagged differently"
  ) ==
    check_total(
      "speed_filter", "trip",
      "tracks with an outlier second to last, flagged differently"
    ),
  check_total(
    "trip_split", "both", "other locations in a trip in only one package"
  ) == 0
)
trip_version <- benchmark$session$value[benchmark$session$item == "trip"]
```

```{r read_timings, include = FALSE}
operation_labels <- c(
  distance = "Step distances",
  speed_filter = "Speed filter",
  trip_split = "Trips"
)
package_levels <- c("tidytracks", "move2", "amt", "trip", "track2KBA")
timings <- benchmark$timings %>%
  mutate(
    total = tracks * locations,
    data_set = paste(
      format(tracks, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE), "tracks of",
      format(locations, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE), "locations"
    ),
    operation = factor(operation_labels[operation], operation_labels),
    package = factor(package, package_levels)
  )
# the two data sets on which the packages are compared
compared <- timings %>%
  filter(
    (tracks == medium[["tracks"]] & locations == medium[["locations"]]) |
      (tracks == long[["tracks"]] & locations == long[["locations"]])
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(tracks)) %>%
  mutate(data_set = factor(data_set, unique(data_set)))
# the two series: tracks of increasing length, and the same total number of
# locations in more and more tracks
longer_tracks <- timings %>%
  filter(tracks == series_tracks)
more_tracks <- timings %>%
  filter(total == series_total)
```

```{r timing_numbers, include = FALSE}
# the time (s) of an operation with a package, on a data set
time_of <- function(operation, package, tracks, locations) {
  timings$seconds[
    timings$operation == operation_labels[[operation]] &
      timings$package == package &
      timings$tracks == tracks &
      timings$locations == locations
  ]
}
# a number with 2 significant digits, for the text
fmt <- function(x) {
  formatC(signif(x, 2), format = "fg", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
}
# the time on a data set, and relative to tidytracks
secs <- function(operation, package, data_set) {
  fmt(time_of(operation, package, data_set[1], data_set[2]))
}
ratio <- function(operation, package, data_set) {
  time_of(operation, package, data_set[1], data_set[2]) /
    time_of(operation, "tidytracks", data_set[1], data_set[2])
}
# the ratios on the two data sets compared, e.g. "2 to 3", or "2" if they are
# the same
ratio_range <- function(operation, package) {
  ratios <- fmt(range(
    ratio(operation, package, medium),
    ratio(operation, package, long)
  ))
  if (ratios[1] == ratios[2]) {
    ratios[1]
  } else {
    paste(ratios[1], "to", ratios[2])
  }
}
```

```{r growth_numbers, include = FALSE}
track_lengths <- sort(unique(longer_tracks$locations))
longest <- max(track_lengths)
track_counts <- sort(unique(more_tracks$tracks))
most <- max(track_counts)
# the largest data set (the longest tracks), the data set with the most
# tracks, and the single track
largest <- c(series_tracks, longest)
many <- c(most, series_total / most)
single <- c(1, series_total)
# the time per location (in microseconds) on the largest data set
per_location <- function(operation, package) {
  fmt(
    1e6 * time_of(operation, package, largest[1], largest[2]) /
      prod(largest)
  )
}
# how many times longer an operation takes on tracks 10 times as long, in the
# series of longer tracks
growth <- function(operation, package, locations) {
  fmt(
    time_of(operation, package, series_tracks, 10 * locations) /
      time_of(operation, package, series_tracks, locations)
  )
}
# the overhead of each track (in ms), from the times on the same locations in
# the most tracks and in the series_tracks tracks (rather than in a single
# track, on which some operations take longer, e.g. track2KBA)
per_track <- function(operation, package) {
  many_time <- time_of(operation, package, many[1], many[2])
  few_time <- time_of(
    operation, package, series_tracks, series_total / series_tracks
  )
  fmt(1000 * (many_time - few_time) / (most - series_tracks))
}
# the time that track2KBA would take on the largest data set (in minutes),
# from its time on a single track of the same length
kba_largest <- round(
  series_tracks * time_of("trip_split", "track2KBA", 1, longest) / 60
)
```

```{r summary_numbers, include = FALSE}
# the range of the times of the other packages relative to tidytracks, for
# the step distances on the two data sets compared
distance_ratios <- fmt(range(vapply(
  c("move2", "amt", "trip"),
  function(package) {
    c(ratio("distance", package, medium), ratio("distance", package, long))
  },
  numeric(2)
)))
# the text below assumes that the overhead of each track is less than a
# millisecond for the trips of tidytracks, and that the time of its speed
# filter hardly depends on the number of tracks (within 50% between a single
# track and the most tracks, with the same locations)
speed_filter_times <- c(
  time_of("speed_filter", "tidytracks", single[1], single[2]),
  time_of("speed_filter", "tidytracks", many[1], many[2])
)
stopifnot(
  as.numeric(per_track("trip_split", "tidytracks")) < 1,
  max(speed_filter_times) < 1.5 * min(speed_filter_times)
)
```

```{r plot_functions, include = FALSE}
# one colour per package
package_colours <- c(
  tidytracks = "#2a78d6",
  move2 = "#8e5bd0",
  amt = "#eb6834",
  trip = "#1baf7a",
  track2KBA = "#c4373b"
)
# the times of a series of data sets, with one panel per operation
series_plot <- function(data, x, x_label) {
  # nolint next: object_usage_linter.
  ggplot(data, aes(x = {{ x }}, y = seconds, colour = package)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
    geom_point(size = 2.5) +
    facet_wrap(~operation, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
    scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
    scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_number(drop0trailing = TRUE)) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = package_colours) +
    labs(x = x_label, y = "Time (s, log scale)", colour = NULL) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.spacing.x = unit(1.5, "lines"),
      # room for the last label of the x axis
      plot.margin = margin(5.5, 15, 5.5, 5.5),
      legend.position = "top"
    )
}
```

## Summary

- Given the same settings, the packages give the same results, except at
  the ends of some tracks and trips, and up to the differences between
  geodesic distances and distances on a sphere.
- `tidytracks` is the fastest for the three operations: for the step
  distances, the other packages take `r distance_ratios[1]` to
  `r distance_ratios[2]` times as long, and `track2KBA` takes
  `r ratio_range("trip_split", "track2KBA")` times as long to split the
  tracks into trips. Its speed filter runs the same algorithm as that of
  `trip`, which takes `r ratio_range("speed_filter", "trip")` times as long.
- The time of `tidytracks` grows in proportion to the number of locations.
  It computes the step distances and runs the speed filter on all the tracks
  at once, so their times hardly depend on the number of tracks, and its
  trip splitting adds less than a millisecond per track
  (`r per_track("trip_split", "tidytracks")` ms), whereas `amt` adds
  `r per_track("distance", "amt")` ms per track to the step distances, and
  `trip` `r per_track("speed_filter", "trip")` ms to the speed filter. This
  overhead matters only for data sets with many short tracks.

The packages are compared on two data sets of simulated tracks, as in the
[home range benchmark](hr_benchmark.html): many tracks of medium length
(`r format(medium[["tracks"]], big.mark = ",")` tracks of
`r format(medium[["locations"]], big.mark = ",")` locations), and a few long
tracks (`r format(long[["tracks"]], big.mark = ",")` tracks of
`r format(long[["locations"]], big.mark = ",")` locations), with the same
settings in all the packages. Two series of data sets then show how the times
grow with the length and the number of the tracks (see
[The data sets](#the-data-sets) and
[Running the operations](#running-the-operations)).

## Do the packages give the same results?

```{r table_checks, echo = FALSE}
tibble::tribble(
  ~operation, ~package, ~difference,
  "Step distances", "move2",
  paste0(
    "up to ", signif(distance_diff("move2"), 2), "% (on a sphere)"
  ),
  "Step distances", "amt",
  paste0("up to ", signif(distance_diff("amt"), 2), "% (on a sphere)"),
  "Step distances", "trip", "none (up to rounding errors)",
  "Speed filter", "trip",
  paste0(
    count("speed_filter", "trip", "locations flagged differently"),
    " of ", count("speed_filter", "tidytracks", "locations flagged"),
    " flagged locations, in ",
    count("speed_filter", "trip", "tracks with locations flagged differently"),
    " tracks"
  ),
  "Trips", "track2KBA",
  paste0(
    "only at the ends of trips (",
    count("trip_split", "track2KBA", "returns to the nest in a trip"),
    " locations) and of tracks (",
    count("trip_split", "tidytracks", "trips of the last location of a track"),
    " trips)"
  )
) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Operation", "Package", "Difference from tidytracks"),
    align = "lll",
    caption = "Differences between the results, over all the data sets."
  )
```

- **Step distances**: `move2` and `amt` measure the steps on a sphere rather
  than on the ellipsoid (with `sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)`, they give the same
  distances as `tidytracks`).
- **Speed filter**: the locations flagged differently are in tracks whose
  second-to-last location is an outlier. `tidytracks` then flags the
  locations before the outlier, one at a time, until the speeds to the outlier
  are low enough, whereas `trip` (in version `r trip_version`) flags only the
  location just before it, as it computes the speeds between locations two
  steps apart wrongly for longitudes and latitudes. Neither package can flag
  the first two and last two locations of a track, whose speeds are not
  computed by the filter: `r count("speed_filter", "both", "outliers among the first two or last two locations of a track")`
  of the `r count("speed_filter", "both", "outliers")` simulated outliers are
  among them, and other locations of the same tracks are flagged instead
  (`check_first_last = TRUE` makes `tidytracks` also check the first and last
  locations).
- **Trips**: `track2KBA` includes in each trip the first location back within
  5 km of the nest, and, when the last location of a track is the first one
  beyond 5 km of the nest, `tidytracks` makes it a trip of its own (an
  incomplete one), whereas `track2KBA` does not.

## How long do they take?

```{r plot_timings, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
ggplot(compared, aes(x = seconds, y = package, colour = package)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  # each operation with its own packages
  facet_grid(operation ~ data_set, scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_number(drop0trailing = TRUE)) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = package_colours, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Time (s, log scale)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing.x = unit(2, "lines"),
    strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0),
    panel.border = element_rect(
      colour = "grey70",
      fill = NA,
      linewidth = 0.5
    )
  )
```

```{r table_timings, echo = FALSE}
# one column per package; empty for the packages that do not have an
# operation
compared %>%
  mutate(
    seconds = formatC(signif(seconds, 2), format = "fg", digits = 2)
  ) %>%
  select(data_set, operation, package, seconds) %>%
  arrange(data_set, operation, package) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = package, values_from = seconds, values_fill = "") %>%
  select(data_set, operation, any_of(package_levels)) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Data set", "Operation",
      intersect(package_levels, levels(droplevels(compared$package)))
    ),
    align = "llrrrrr",
    caption = paste(
      "Time (s) of each operation on all the tracks of each data set",
      "(median of three to ten runs)."
    )
  )
```

- **Step distances**: `tidytracks` is the fastest: `move2` takes
  `r ratio_range("distance", "move2")` times as long, `amt`
  `r ratio_range("distance", "amt")` times and `trip`
  `r ratio_range("distance", "trip")` times. `tidytracks` computes the
  distances of all the tracks at once (with `geodist`), whereas `amt` and
  `trip` measure each track in turn.
- **Speed filter**: `tidytracks` and `trip` run the same algorithm, in R, but
  `trip` filters each track in turn, and computes the speeds between all the
  remaining locations again in each pass of the filter, whereas `tidytracks`
  filters all the tracks at once, only computes again the speeds around the
  locations removed in the previous pass, and only computes geodesic
  distances where the speeds could exceed the maximum (which it finds with a
  fast upper bound of the distances): `trip` takes
  `r ratio_range("speed_filter", "trip")` times as long.
- **Trips**: `track2KBA` takes `r ratio_range("trip_split", "track2KBA")`
  times as long as `tidytracks`, as it goes through the locations of each
  track one at a time, in R.

## How the times grow

### Longer tracks

```{r plot_longer_tracks, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.4}
series_plot(
  longer_tracks,
  locations,
  paste0(
    "Locations per track (", series_tracks, " tracks, log scale)"
  )
)
```

With `r series_tracks` tracks, the time of the operations grows about in
proportion to the number of locations: on the `r fmt(prod(largest))`
locations of the largest data set, `tidytracks` takes about
`r per_location("distance", "tidytracks")` µs per location for the step
distances, `r per_location("speed_filter", "tidytracks")` µs for the speed
filter, and `r per_location("trip_split", "tidytracks")` µs for the trips.
The time of
`track2KBA` grows faster than the length of the tracks, as it updates the
whole track at many of its steps: with tracks ten
times as long (from `r fmt(track_lengths[1])` to `r fmt(track_lengths[2])`
locations), it takes `r growth("trip_split", "track2KBA", track_lengths[1])`
times as long. It was thus not run on the largest data set, on which it would
take more than `r kba_largest` minutes.

### More tracks

```{r plot_more_tracks, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.4}
series_plot(
  more_tracks,
  tracks,
  paste0(
    "Number of tracks (", fmt(series_total), " locations in all, log scale)"
  )
)
```

With the same `r fmt(series_total)` locations in more and more tracks, the
time of the operations that handle each track in turn grows with the number
of tracks. `tidytracks` and `move2` compute the step distances of all the
tracks at once, so their time hardly depends on the number of tracks
(`r secs("distance", "tidytracks", many)` s with `tidytracks` for
`r fmt(most)` tracks, against `r secs("distance", "tidytracks", single)` s
for a single track), whereas `amt` and `trip` add about
`r per_track("distance", "amt")` ms and `r per_track("distance", "trip")` ms
per track. Likewise, the speed filter of `tidytracks` runs on all the tracks
at once (`r secs("speed_filter", "tidytracks", many)` s for `r fmt(most)`
tracks, against `r secs("speed_filter", "tidytracks", single)` s for a single
track), whereas `trip` adds about `r per_track("speed_filter", "trip")` ms
per track. Trip splitting adds about
`r per_track("trip_split", "tidytracks")` ms per track with `tidytracks`.
`track2KBA` adds the trips of each track to those of the previous tracks with
`rbind()`, which copies them all each time, so it takes
`r secs("trip_split", "track2KBA", many)` s on the `r fmt(most)` tracks.

# How the benchmark was run

The benchmark takes about `r round(benchmark$run_minutes / 5) * 5` minutes to
run, so it was run once with the script
`vignettes/articles/code/operations_benchmark.R` (in the source code of the
package), and its results are read here from
`vignettes/articles/benchmark-results.rds`. The code shown below is taken
from that script. Timings depend on the machine (see
[Machine and software](#machine-and-software)), but the differences between
the packages, and how the times grow with the size of the data, should be
similar on other machines.

The benchmark uses these packages:

```{r packages, message = FALSE}
```

## Simulating tracks

The tracks are those of a central place forager, such as a seabird breeding
in a colony, with a GPS location every 5 minutes. They are simulated, so that
data sets of any size can be made with the same properties:

```{r simulate-tracks}
```

For example, the first two days of three tracks (the black points are the
nests, and the lines that leave the map go to outliers):

```{r example_tracks, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3}
example_tracks <- simulate_tracks(n_tracks = 3, n_locations = 576, seed = 1)
ggplot(example_tracks, aes(lon, lat)) +
  geom_path(colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(
    aes(nest_lon, nest_lat),
    data = distinct(example_tracks, id, nest_lon, nest_lat),
    colour = "black",
    size = 2
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~id) +
  coord_quickmap(
    xlim = mean(example_tracks$nest_lon) + c(-1.4, 1.4),
    ylim = mean(example_tracks$nest_lat) + c(-0.8, 0.8)
  ) +
  labs(x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

## The data sets

The time taken by an operation on a set of tracks has two parts: one that
grows with the number of locations, and an overhead for each track (e.g. to
select its locations, or to build its results). The benchmark uses two series
of data sets: tracks of increasing length (with the same number of tracks),
and the same total number of locations split into an increasing number of
tracks (from a single long track to many short ones):

```{r data-sets, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r data-sets-table, eval = FALSE}
```

Two of these data sets, many tracks of medium length and a few long tracks,
are those on which the packages are compared:

```{r table_data_sets, echo = FALSE}
data_sets <- benchmark$timings %>%
  distinct(tracks, locations) %>%
  mutate(
    total = tracks * locations,
    days = locations * 5 / (60 * 24),
    comparison = case_when(
      tracks == long[["tracks"]] & locations == long[["locations"]] ~
        "long tracks",
      tracks == medium[["tracks"]] & locations == medium[["locations"]] ~
        "medium tracks",
      TRUE ~ ""
    ),
    series = case_when(
      tracks == series_tracks & total == series_total ~ "both",
      tracks == series_tracks ~ "longer tracks",
      TRUE ~ "more tracks"
    )
  )
stopifnot(sum(data_sets$comparison != "") == 2)
data_sets %>%
  # the series of longer tracks first, then the other data sets
  arrange(tracks != series_tracks, tracks, locations) %>%
  mutate(
    across(
      c(tracks, locations, total),
      ~ formatC(.x, format = "d", big.mark = ",")
    ),
    days = formatC(signif(days, 2), format = "fg", digits = 2)
  ) %>%
  select(tracks, locations, days, total, comparison, series) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Tracks", "Locations per track", "Days per track", "Total locations",
      "Comparison", "Series"
    ),
    align = "rrrrll"
  )
```

## Running the operations

Each package works on its own class of objects: a `move2` object for
`tidytracks` and `move2`, a `track_xyt` for `amt`, a `trip` object (a
`SpatialPointsDataFrame` from `sp`) for `trip`, and data frames for
`track2KBA`. These are built from the data frame of locations of each data
set (outside of the timings):

```{r inputs, eval = FALSE}
```

The operations are then run with each package, on all the tracks of a data
set:

```{r operations, eval = FALSE}
```

The settings are matched so that the packages give the same results:

- **Step distances**: `tidytracks` and `trip` compute geodesic distances on
  the WGS84 ellipsoid (with the `geodist` package), whereas `move2` and `amt`
  use `sf::st_distance()`, which, with `s2` (the default of `sf`), computes
  great circle distances on a sphere. `tidytracks`, `move2` and `amt` give
  `NA` for the last location of each track, and `trip` gives 0. `amt` measures
  the steps of a single track, so its tracks are nested and measured in
  turn, as in its documentation, and this is included in its time.
- **Speed filter**: `tidytracks` and `trip` run the same algorithm, with a
  maximum speed of 120 km/h (`trip` takes it in km/h, for longitudes and
  latitudes). The optional check of the first and last locations of each
  track of `tidytracks` is off by default.
- **Trips**: both packages use the nest of each animal, start a trip when
  the animal goes further than 5 km from it, end it when it comes back
  within 5 km, and keep the locations at the nest. `track2KBA` drops trips
  shorter than a minimum duration, which is set to 0 here, as `tidytracks`
  has none.

Each operation is run once, as a warm-up, which also gives the results
compared, and then, if that took less than a minute, again until these runs
have taken a minute (but at least three and at most ten times), of which the
median time is reported:

```{r timing, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r run-benchmark, eval = FALSE}
```

The results of each package are then compared with those of `tidytracks`, on
each data set:

```{r checks, eval = FALSE}
```

## From the results to the tables and plots

The benchmark saves its results in `benchmark-results.rds`, which is read and
summarised for the [results](#results) above with this code:

```{r, ref.label = c("results_packages", "data_set_roles", "read_timings"), eval = FALSE}
```

and the plots of the timings are drawn with:

```{r, ref.label = c("plot_functions", "plot_timings", "plot_longer_tracks", "plot_more_tracks"), eval = FALSE}
```

## Running the benchmark again

To run the benchmark again (e.g. after changing `tidytracks`, or on another
machine), install `tidytracks` (with `R CMD INSTALL`, rather than loading it
with `devtools::load_all()`, which compiles its C++ code without
optimisation) and the other packages, and run, on an otherwise idle machine:

```sh
cd vignettes/articles
Rscript code/operations_benchmark.R
```

which overwrites `benchmark-results.rds`; then render this article again.
`Rscript code/operations_benchmark.R quick` runs everything on a few small
data sets in less than a minute, to check the script, and saves its results
in a temporary directory instead.
